questions.stem: In a transverse wave, how do the particles of the medium move compared with the direction of energy transfer?
options: They oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer
They travel along with the wave in the direction of energy transfer
They move in circles centred on the direction of energy transfer
They oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
questions.explanation: In a transverse wave, such as a wave on a rope, each particle oscillates at right angles to the direction the energy travels. Oscillation parallel to the energy transfer is what defines a longitudinal wave.

questions.stem: A student pushes and pulls one end of a stretched slinky spring back and forth along its length. What kind of wave does this produce?
options: A transverse wave, with the coils oscillating perpendicular to the energy transfer
A longitudinal wave, with the coils oscillating perpendicular to the energy transfer
A transverse wave, with the coils oscillating parallel to the energy transfer
A longitudinal wave, with the coils oscillating parallel to the energy transfer
questions.explanation: Moving the end along the spring's length makes the coils bunch up and spread out, forming compressions and rarefactions. The coils oscillate along the direction the energy travels, so the wave is longitudinal. Shaking the end side to side would make a transverse wave.

questions.stem: A wave travels along a rope from one end to the other. What happens to a small piece of tape stuck to the middle of the rope?
options: It moves forward a little with each crest and stays in the new spot
It oscillates about a fixed position while energy passes along the rope
It travels along the rope with the wave and reaches the far end
It stays completely still because only energy moves along the rope
questions.explanation: A wave transfers energy, not matter. Each part of the rope oscillates about its equilibrium position as the wave passes, then returns to rest. The tape moves, but it does not travel along with the wave.

questions.stem: What is the amplitude of a transverse wave?
options: The distance between two neighbouring crests
The number of crests passing a point each second
The maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position
The vertical distance from a crest to the next trough
questions.explanation: Amplitude is measured from the equilibrium (rest) position to a crest or to a trough. The crest-to-trough distance is twice the amplitude. The distance between neighbouring crests is the wavelength, and crests per second is the frequency.

questions.stem: How is the wavelength of a longitudinal wave measured?
options: From the rest position of a particle to its maximum displacement
From the front of one compression to the back of the same compression
From the centre of one compression to the centre of the next
From the centre of a compression to the centre of the next rarefaction
questions.explanation: A wavelength is the length of one complete cycle, such as between adjacent compressions or adjacent rarefactions. From a compression to the next rarefaction is only half a wavelength.

questions.stem: The vertical distance from a crest to a trough of a water wave is 0.40 m, and adjacent crests are 3.0 m apart. What are its amplitude and wavelength?
options: Amplitude 0.40 m, wavelength 3.0 m
Amplitude 0.20 m, wavelength 1.5 m
Amplitude 0.40 m, wavelength 6.0 m
Amplitude 0.20 m, wavelength 3.0 m
questions.explanation: The amplitude is half the crest-to-trough height: 0.40/2 = 0.20 m. The wavelength is the crest-to-crest distance, 3.0 m. Halving the crest spacing would give the crest-to-trough horizontal distance, half a wavelength.

questions.stem: A wave has a period of 0.025 s. What is its frequency?
options: 40 Hz
25 Hz
4.0 Hz
questions.explanation: f = 1/T = 1/0.025 = 40 Hz. Frequency and period are reciprocals: a short period means many cycles each second.

questions.stem: A sound wave of frequency 680 Hz travels at 340 m s⁻¹ in air. What is its wavelength?
questions.explanation: v = fλ, so λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.50 m. Dividing the frequency by the speed gives 2.0, and multiplying them gives 2.3 × 10⁵.

questions.stem: A float on a lake bobs up and down 15 times in 5.0 s. The crests of the waves are 1.5 m apart. What is the speed of the waves?
options: 2.0 m s⁻¹
4.5 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: The frequency is 15/5.0 = 3.0 Hz and the wavelength is 1.5 m, so v = fλ = 3.0 × 1.5 = 4.5 m s⁻¹. Multiplying the 15 oscillations by 1.5 m gives 22.5, which forgets to divide by the time.

questions.stem: A signal generator drives a speaker in air. The frequency is doubled while the amplitude stays the same. What happens to the sound wave?
options: Its speed doubles and its wavelength stays the same
Its wavelength doubles and its speed stays the same
Its speed and wavelength both stay the same
Its wavelength halves and its speed stays the same
questions.explanation: The speed of sound depends on the medium, not on the source, so it stays constant. From v = fλ, doubling f must halve λ. The pitch rises; the loudness is set by the unchanged amplitude.

questions.stem: A microphone records a sound in air whose displacement-time graph has a period of 2.5 ms. The speed of sound in the air is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the wavelength of the sound?
questions.explanation: First f = 1/T = 1/0.0025 = 400 Hz, then λ = v/f = 340/400 = 0.85 m; equivalently λ = vT. Dividing the speed by the period gives 1.4 × 10⁵, and 136 comes from dividing 340 by 2.5 without converting milliseconds.

questions.stem: A 500 Hz sound passes from air, where it travels at 340 m s⁻¹, into water, where it travels at 1500 m s⁻¹. What is its wavelength in the water?
questions.explanation: The frequency is set by the source and does not change when the wave enters a new medium; the speed changes, so the wavelength does. λ = 1500/500 = 3.0 m. The value 0.68 m is the wavelength in air.

questions.stem: Which two quantities can be read directly from a displacement-time graph for one particle in a wave?
options: Speed and wavelength
Period and amplitude
Wavelength and amplitude
Wavelength and period
questions.explanation: A displacement-time graph follows one particle over time, so the time for one cycle (the period) and the maximum displacement (the amplitude) can be read from it. The wavelength is a distance, so it needs a displacement-distance graph.

questions.stem: Which two quantities can be read directly from a displacement-distance graph of a wave at one instant?
options: Period and frequency
Wavelength and amplitude
Period and amplitude
Frequency and wavelength
questions.explanation: A displacement-distance graph is a snapshot of the whole wave at one moment. It shows the length of one cycle in space (wavelength) and the maximum displacement (amplitude). Period and frequency involve time, so they come from a displacement-time graph.

questions.stem: For a sound wave, a displacement-time graph shows a period of 4.0 ms and a displacement-distance graph shows a wavelength of 1.36 m. What is the speed of the wave?
options: 5.4 m s⁻¹
184 m s⁻¹
340 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: f = 1/T = 1/0.0040 = 250 Hz, and v = fλ = 250 × 1.36 = 340 m s⁻¹. Multiplying the period by the wavelength gives 5.4 × 10⁻³ in seconds, or 5.4 if milliseconds are left unconverted.

questions.stem: A displacement-distance graph shows a transverse wave travelling to the right. Point P is at zero displacement, with a crest just to its left and a trough to its right. How is P moving at this instant?
options: Downward at its maximum speed, as the trough approaches it
It is momentarily at rest, because its displacement is zero
To the right, at the same speed as the wave travels
Upward at its maximum speed, as the crest approaches it
questions.explanation: The wave moves right, so the crest now just to the left of P is about to arrive there; P must be rising. At zero displacement a particle in a wave is moving fastest. In a transverse wave the particles move up and down, never along with the wave.

questions.stem: On a displacement-distance graph for a longitudinal wave, displacement to the right is positive. Where along the wave is there a compression?
options: Where the displacement is zero and the graph slopes upward
Where the displacement is at its maximum positive value
Where the displacement is at its maximum negative value
Where the displacement is zero and the graph slopes downward
questions.explanation: Where the graph crosses zero sloping downward, particles just to the left are displaced right and particles just to the right are displaced left, so they crowd together into a compression. Where it slopes upward, they move apart into a rarefaction. Peaks on the graph are not compressions, a common misreading.

questions.stem: An electric bell rings inside a sealed jar while the air is pumped out. Why does the sound fade, even though the bell can still be seen vibrating?
options: Sound is an electromagnetic wave and needs air to carry its fields
The bell vibrates with a lower frequency when the air is removed
Light and sound both need a medium, but light needs much less of it
Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium to travel through
questions.explanation: Sound travels as vibrations passed from particle to particle, so without a medium it cannot propagate. Light is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium, which is why the bell is still visible.

questions.stem: How does a sound wave transfer energy through air?
options: Air particles vibrate up and down at right angles to the wave, passing energy along like a rope wave
Oscillating electric and magnetic fields in the air carry the energy from the source to the listener
Air particles vibrate back and forth and pass energy to their neighbours, forming compressions and rarefactions
Air particles travel from the source to the listener, carrying the energy with them as they flow along
questions.explanation: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave: each particle oscillates along the direction of travel and pushes on its neighbours, so regions of high and low pressure travel outward. The particles themselves do not travel to the listener. Oscillating fields describe electromagnetic waves, not sound.

questions.stem: Which property of a sound wave determines its pitch, and which determines its loudness?
options: Amplitude determines pitch; frequency determines loudness
Wavelength determines pitch; speed determines loudness
Speed determines pitch; wavelength determines loudness
Frequency determines pitch; amplitude determines loudness
questions.explanation: A higher frequency is heard as a higher pitch, and a larger amplitude as a louder sound. The speed of sound is set by the medium and is the same for all pitches in air.

questions.stem: Two sounds from a speaker have the same frequency, but the second has a larger amplitude. How does the energy carried by the second compare?
options: It carries the same energy, because the energy of a sound depends only on its frequency
It carries less energy, because the particles take longer to complete each vibration
It carries more energy, because a larger amplitude makes the sound travel faster
It carries more energy, because the air particles vibrate with larger displacements
questions.explanation: The energy of a sound wave increases with its amplitude: particles vibrating through larger displacements carry more energy, heard as a louder sound. Amplitude does not change the period or the speed of the wave.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares light with sound?
options: Both need a medium, but light travels about a million times faster than sound in air
Neither needs a medium, but sound travels more slowly because its waves are longitudinal
Light needs no medium and travels at 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum; sound needs a medium
Light needs a medium and travels at 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in air only; sound needs no medium
questions.explanation: Light is an electromagnetic wave: oscillating electric and magnetic fields that can travel through a vacuum at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Sound is a mechanical wave and cannot travel through a vacuum.

questions.stem: How are electromagnetic waves produced and how do they carry energy?
options: Stationary charges produce steady electric and magnetic fields that point along the direction the wave travels
Accelerating charges produce oscillating electric and magnetic fields that both point along the direction of travel
Accelerating charges produce oscillating electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel
Vibrating particles produce compressions and rarefactions in the medium, which pass energy from particle to particle
questions.explanation: An oscillating or accelerating charge produces changing electric and magnetic fields, each of which regenerates the other. The fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, so EM waves are transverse. Compressions and rarefactions describe sound, which needs a medium.

questions.stem: Which list places parts of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency?
options: Microwave, radio, visible, infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray
Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray
X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio
Radio, infrared, microwave, visible, X-ray, ultraviolet
questions.explanation: In order of increasing frequency (and decreasing wavelength), the spectrum runs radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma. The reverse list is in order of increasing wavelength.

questions.stem: As you move along the electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves towards gamma rays, what happens?
options: Wavelength decreases and frequency increases, while speed in a vacuum increases
Wavelength decreases, while frequency and photon energy increase
Wavelength increases, while frequency and photon energy decrease
Wavelength and frequency both increase, while photon energy is constant
questions.explanation: All EM waves travel at c in a vacuum, so from c = fλ a shorter wavelength means a higher frequency, and from E = hf a higher frequency means more energetic photons. The speed in a vacuum is the same across the whole spectrum.

questions.stem: Orange light has a wavelength of 600 nm. Using c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, what is its frequency?
options: 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz
questions.explanation: f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸/600 × 10⁻⁹ = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Leaving the wavelength in nanometres gives 5.0 × 10⁵ Hz, and dividing λ by c gives 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁵.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz? Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
questions.explanation: E = hf = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5.0 × 10¹⁴ ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Dividing h by f gives 1.3 × 10⁻⁴⁸, and an error in adding the powers of ten gives 3.3 × 10⁻²⁰.

questions.stem: An X-ray has a wavelength of 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Using h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, what is the energy of one X-ray photon?
questions.explanation: First f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸/1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 3.0 × 10¹⁸ Hz, then E = hf ≈ 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ J. Using E = h/λ gives 6.6 × 10⁻²⁴, which leaves out c, and hλ/c gives 2.2 × 10⁻³².

questions.stem: Why are X-rays used to image broken bones?
options: They are emitted by warm bone, so the image shows the temperature of the bone
Their high-energy photons pass through soft tissue but are absorbed more by dense bone
Their long wavelength lets them diffract around bones to form a clear outline on film
Their low-energy photons are reflected by bone and scattered by the soft tissue
questions.explanation: X-ray photons have enough energy to pass through soft tissue, but dense bone absorbs more of them, so bones show as light areas on the image. X-rays have very short wavelengths, so diffraction around bones is not what forms the image. Emission by warm objects describes infrared.

questions.stem: Which use of an electromagnetic region is correctly matched to the property that makes it suitable?
options: Gamma rays carry mobile phone signals because their long wavelength diffracts around buildings
Ultraviolet sterilises surfaces because its high-energy photons damage the DNA of microbes
Radio waves image the inside of the body because their high-energy photons are absorbed by bone
Infrared sterilises medical equipment because its photons have more energy than gamma rays
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet photons have enough energy to damage DNA, killing bacteria and viruses on surfaces. Radio photons have very low energy, infrared photons have less energy than gamma photons, and gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths of all.

questions.stem: Which electromagnetic region do thermal imaging cameras detect?
options: X-ray
Infrared
Ultraviolet
Microwave
questions.explanation: All warm objects emit infrared radiation, and warmer objects emit more, so a thermal camera detecting infrared can show temperature differences, even in the dark.

questions.stem: Why are microwaves used for satellite communication?
options: Their very long wavelengths diffract around the curve of the Earth to reach the satellite
They travel faster through the atmosphere than any other part of the spectrum
They pass through the atmosphere with little absorption and can be sent in narrow beams
Their photons carry enough energy to ionise the upper atmosphere and bounce off it
questions.explanation: Microwaves pass through the atmosphere and clouds with little absorption, and their short wavelength (compared with radio) allows them to be focused into narrow beams by dish antennas. All EM waves travel at about the same speed in air.

questions.stem: Why does the intensity of light from a point source decrease with the square of the distance?
options: The wavelength increases with distance, so each photon carries less energy far away
The same power spreads over the surface of a sphere whose area is proportional to r²
The light loses energy to the air at a rate proportional to the distance travelled
The photons slow down as they travel, so fewer arrive each second at larger distances
questions.explanation: A point source sends its power out in all directions, so at distance r it is spread over a sphere of area 4πr². Doubling r quadruples that area, so the intensity falls to a quarter. Photon speed and wavelength do not change with distance in a vacuum.

questions.stem: A small lamp gives an intensity of 80 W m⁻² at 2.0 m. What is the intensity at 4.0 m?
options: 20 W m⁻²
40 W m⁻²
160 W m⁻²
10 W m⁻²
questions.explanation: I is proportional to 1/r², so doubling the distance divides the intensity by 2² = 4: 80/4 = 20 W m⁻². Halving it to 40 assumes intensity is proportional to 1/r.

questions.stem: A light meter reads 12 units at 3.0 m from a point source. At what distance from the source will it read 3.0 units?
questions.explanation: I₁r₁² = I₂r₂², so r₂ = r₁√(I₁/I₂) = 3.0 × √(12/3.0) = 3.0 × 2 = 6.0 m. Multiplying by 4 instead of √4 gives 12 m, which treats intensity as falling with 1/r.

questions.stem: A detector is moved from 1.0 m to 3.0 m away from a point source of radiation. By what factor does the intensity change?
options: It falls to one-third
It falls to one-sixth
It rises to three times
It falls to one-ninth
questions.explanation: I ∝ 1/r², so tripling the distance changes the intensity by a factor of 1/3² = 1/9. One-third would follow if intensity were proportional to 1/r.

questions.stem: In an experiment, the intensity of a small lamp is measured at several distances r. Which graph should give a straight line through the origin?
options: Intensity against r
Intensity against 1/r²
Intensity against r²
Intensity against 1/r
questions.explanation: Since I = k/r², plotting I against 1/r² linearises the relationship, giving a straight line through the origin with gradient k. Plotting I against r gives a falling curve, from which the relationship is hard to confirm.

questions.stem: A light sensor reads 900 lux at 0.20 m from a small lamp. At 0.30 m it reads 430 lux, but the inverse square law predicts 400 lux. What most likely explains the difference?
options: The inverse square law only holds for sound waves
The lamp's light speeds up as it moves away from it
The sensor reading falls with 1/r instead of 1/r²
Background light in the room is adding to the reading
questions.explanation: The prediction is 900 × (0.20/0.30)² = 400 lux. A higher reading suggests extra light reaching the sensor, such as room light, a systematic error that affects distant readings most. If intensity fell with 1/r the reading would be 600 lux, far above the measurement.
